lessons.body:
A Julia function is a set of *methods*. When you call it, Julia looks at the
runtime types of *all* the arguments and runs the most specific method that
applies. The order in which the methods were defined does not matter, and
neither do the declared types of the variables or containers the values came
from.

If two methods apply and neither is more specific than the other, the call is
ambiguous and throws a `MethodError`. The fix is a method for the intersection,
not reordering definitions.

In the symdiff project, `deriv(t::Mul, x)`, `deriv(t::Pow, x)` and
`deriv(t::Fn{typeof(sin)}, x)` are separate methods of one function. Dispatch
replaces the `if t isa Mul ... elseif ...` chain you might write elsewhere.

checks.code:
f(x::Number) = "number"
f(x::Integer) = "integer"
f(x) = "anything"
println(f(3), " ", f(2.5), " ", f("hi"))
checks.explanation: 3 is an Int, so both `::Number` and `::Integer` apply and `Integer` is more specific. 2.5 is a Float64, a Number but not an Integer. "hi" matches only the untyped method.
checks.hint: For each call, list the methods whose signature accepts the argument, then ask which of those is the narrowest. Definition order plays no part.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how an `if`/`elseif` chain or pattern-match order works, but Julia does not try methods in definition order.
In Python a second `def f` replaces the first. In Julia, a definition with a *different* signature adds a method; only an identical signature replaces one.
Julia never converts arguments to pick a method. 2.5 is a Float64, and Float64 is not a subtype of Integer.

checks.prompt: Three methods of `f`, defined in this order. What is printed?

checks.code:
g(x::Int, y) = 1
g(x, y::Int) = 2
try
    println(g(1, 2))
catch err
    println(typeof(err))
end
checks.explanation: Each method is more specific in one argument, so neither wins and the call is ambiguous. Julia reports this as a `MethodError` whose message says "ambiguous". Defining `g(x::Int, y::Int)` resolves it.
checks.hint: Both methods apply. Is either signature a subtype of the other? If not, Julia refuses to guess, and you are asked for the exception's type.

misconceptions.feedback: Definition order does not break ties between methods.
A later method with a different signature does not override an earlier one; both stay in the method table.
There is no `AmbiguityError` type in Base. Ambiguity is reported as a `MethodError` (read its message).

checks.prompt: Neither method is more specific for `g(1, 2)`. What is printed?

checks.code:
abstract type Shape end
struct Circle <: Shape end
struct Square <: Shape end
collide(a::Shape, b::Shape) = "generic"
collide(a::Circle, b::Square) = "circle-square"
collide(a::Square, b::Circle) = "square-circle"
shapes = Shape[Circle(), Square()]
println(collide(shapes[2], shapes[1]))
checks.explanation: `shapes[2]` is a Square and `shapes[1]` a Circle at run time. The container's element type `Shape` does not hide that. Julia picks `collide(::Square, ::Circle)`.
checks.hint: Dispatch uses the type of each *value* at the moment of the call. What are the types of the two values passed, and in which order?

misconceptions.feedback: In Java or C++, overloads are chosen from declared (static) types, which would give the generic method. Julia dispatches on runtime types.
Dispatch is on the ordered tuple of argument types; (Square, Circle) and (Circle, Square) are different signatures.
Values taken out of a `Vector{Shape}` keep their concrete types, so the specific methods apply.

lessons.title: Multiple dispatch: the most specific method wins, on all arguments

lessons.body:
A *concrete* type can have instances (Float64, Vector{Float64}, your structs);
an *abstract* type (Real, AbstractVector, Term) only groups other types. The
compiler generates fast code when it knows concrete types: the layout of a
value, which method to call, whether a value fits in a register.

Two places where novices accidentally lose that knowledge:

* containers: `[]` has no elements to infer from, so it is a `Vector{Any}`;
* struct fields: `x::Real` means "any Real", so every read checks the type at
  run time.

Note the difference between an abstract *element* type and an abstract
*container* type: `Vector{Real}` is concrete (a vector of boxed Reals), while
`Vector` without a parameter is not a concrete type at all.

Parametric types are *invariant*: `Vector{Int}` is not a subtype of
`Vector{Integer}`. Write `Vector{<:Integer}` for "a vector of some Integer type".

In the symdiff project, `Add.args::Vector{Term}` is deliberate. It is a concrete
container of an abstract element type, because a tree mixes node kinds. The
`evaluate` methods restore type stability with `::T` assertions.

checks.explanation: `[]` is `Vector{Any}`. To get an empty vector of a specific type, write `Float64[]` or `Vector{Float64}()`.
checks.hint: An empty literal gives Julia no element to infer a type from. Which element type accepts anything that might be pushed into it later?

misconceptions.feedback: `Nothing` is the type of the value `nothing`; a vector of it could only ever hold `nothing`s.
`Union{}` (the type with no values) is what inference uses for code that never returns. An empty literal gets the most permissive element type instead.
Like a Python list, it can hold anything, but Julia still gives it a full type with an element type and a dimension.

checks.explanation: `Vector{Real}` is concrete: `Real[1, 2.5]` is an instance (its elements are boxed). `Vector` alone is a `UnionAll` (the element type is missing), and `Real` is abstract.
checks.hint: Can you create an instance of `Vector{Real}`? Of `Vector` without saying what it holds? Concreteness is about whether the type itself can have instances.

misconceptions.feedback: An abstract *parameter* does not make the container abstract. `Vector{Real}` is one specific concrete type.
`Vector` without a parameter stands for every `Vector{T}`. It is not itself a type with instances.
`Vector` without a parameter stands for every `Vector{T}`. It is not itself a type with instances.

checks.explanation: Parametric types are invariant: `Vector{Int}` is not a `Vector{Integer}` even though `Int <: Integer`. `Vector{<:Integer}` means "`Vector{T}` for some `T <: Integer`", which includes it.
checks.hint: A `Vector{Integer}` must accept `push!(v, big(1))`. Could a `Vector{Int}` honour that promise?

misconceptions.feedback: Java arrays and Python's typing for read-only sequences are covariant; Julia's parametric types are not.
`Vector{<:Integer}` is shorthand for `Vector{T} where T<:Integer`, which `Vector{Int}` belongs to.
Both halves are backwards: invariance rejects the first, the `<:` wildcard accepts the second.

checks.code:
struct A
    x::Real
end
struct B{T<:Real}
    x::T
end
println(fieldtype(A, :x), " ", fieldtype(B{Float64}, :x), " ", isconcretetype(fieldtype(A, :x)))
checks.explanation: `A.x` is declared `Real` for every `A`, whatever value it holds, so code reading it cannot know the concrete type. `B{Float64}.x` is `Float64` because the parameter fixes it. The checker rule JT002 points at fields like `A.x`.
checks.hint: A field's type comes from the declaration (and the type parameters), never from a value stored later. What did each declaration say?

misconceptions.feedback: Storing a Float64 in `A(1.5).x` does not change the declared field type, which is still `Real`.
In `B{Float64}`, `T` is `Float64`, so the field `x::T` has type `Float64`.
`isconcretetype` asks about the declared type `Real`, which is abstract regardless of what is stored.

holes.spec:
deriv(t::Mul, x::Sym) -> Term

n-ary product rule: d(a₁·a₂·…·aₙ)/dx = Σᵢ a₁·…·(daᵢ/dx)·…·aₙ, as an `Add` of
`n` `Mul`s. Must not mutate `t` (or `t.args`).
holes.summary: deriv(t::Mul, x): the n-ary product rule, without mutating the input
match_pattern(p::PVar, t, b): bind a pattern variable consistently

holes.spec:
is_size_decreasing(r::Rule) -> Bool

`true` when *every* instance of `r` strictly shrinks the term's `nodecount`, which
proves that rewriting with a set of such rules terminates under any strategy.

Condition: `nodecount(r.lhs) > nodecount(r.rhs)` **and** every pattern variable
occurs in `r.rhs` at most as many times as in `r.lhs` (a variable duplicated on
the right can be bound to an arbitrarily large term).

Why it suffices: for a substitution σ, size(lσ) − size(rσ) =
(size(l) − size(r)) + Σᵥ (occₗ(v) − occᵣ(v))·(size(σv) − 1) > 0, and replacing a
subterm by a smaller one shrinks the whole term.
holes.summary: is_size_decreasing(r): a termination argument for rewrite rules

holes.spec:
mk_add(args::Vector{Term}) -> Term

Canonical sum of already-canonical `args`:

1. Flatten: an `Add` among `args` contributes its own arguments.
2. Fold all `Const`s into one rational constant `c`.
3. Write every other summand as `k * rest` (see `coeff_and_rest`) and combine
   summands with equal `rest` by adding their `k`s. Drop those whose `k` is 0.
4. Rebuild each summand as `rest` (when `k == 1`) or `mk_mul(Term[Const(k), rest])`,
   in increasing `isless` order of `rest`.
5. Return `Const(c)` if nothing else is left; the single summand if `c == 0` and
   only one is left; otherwise `Add` with `Const(c)` first (omitted when `c == 0`).

Examples: `x + x -> 2x`, `3x + y - 3x -> y`, `1 + x + 2 -> 3 + x`.
holes.summary: mk_add(args): flatten, fold constants, collect like terms, sort

holes.spec:
deriv(t::Fn{F}, x::Sym) -> Term

Chain rule: d f(u)/dx = f'(u) · du/dx. The outer derivative f'(u) is `dfn(f, u)`,
where `f = func(t)` and `u = t.arg`.
holes.summary: deriv(t::Fn{F}, x): the chain rule via dfn

holes.spec:
rewrite_budgeted!(budget::Ref{Int}, t, rules) -> Term

Innermost rewriting. First rewrite every child of `t` (use `map_children`). Then
try the rules *in order* at the root; for the first whose `lhs` matches, spend one
step of `budget` (if `budget[]` would go below zero, throw
`error("rewrite: step budget exhausted")`), substitute the bindings into its
`rhs`, and rewrite *that result* again, because it may contain new redexes. If no
rule matches, return the term. Mutates only `budget`, which by Julia's
convention for `!` functions comes first.
holes.summary: rewrite_budgeted!(budget, t, rules): innermost rewriting to a normal form

holes.spec:
dp54_step!(c::DP54Cache, f!, t, y, h) -> nothing

One Dormand-Prince 5(4) step of size `h` from `(t, y)`.

On entry `c.k1` must hold `f(t, y)` (the caller evaluates it once; after an
accepted step it is the previous step's `k7`). The step evaluates stages 2 to
7: stage `i` is `f!(c.ki, ytmp, t + Ci*h)` with
`ytmp = y + h * (Ai1*k1 + ... + Ai(i-1)*k(i-1))`, using the constants
`A21` ... `A76` and `C2` ... `C5` of this module (stages 6 and 7 are at
`t + h`). Stage 7 is evaluated at the new solution itself.

On return:
* `c.ynew` is the 5th-order solution `y + h * (A71*k1 + A73*k3 + ... + A76*k6)`
  at `t + h`;
* `c.k7` is `f(t + h, c.ynew)`;
* `c.err` is the error estimate `y5 - y4 = h * (E1*k1 + E3*k3 + ... + E7*k7)`.

`y` is not modified. Exactly 6 calls to `f!`; allocates nothing (use
in-place broadcasts such as `@. c.ytmp = y + h * (A21 * c.k1)`).
holes.summary: dp54_step!(c, f!, t, y, h): one Dormand-Prince 5(4) step with its error estimate

holes.spec:
error_norm(err, y, ynew, atol, rtol) -> Float64

The scaled root-mean-square norm an adaptive step is judged by (Hairer I,
eq. II.4.11):

    sqrt( (1/n) * sum_i ( err[i] / sc[i] )^2 ),   sc[i] = atol + rtol * max(|y[i]|, |ynew[i]|)

A value <= 1 means the step meets the tolerance. Scaling each component by
its own size makes the test relative where the solution is large and
absolute where it is near zero. Allocates nothing.
holes.summary: error_norm(err, y, ynew, atol, rtol): the scaled RMS norm a step is judged by

holes.spec:
kepler_exact(e, t) -> Vector{Float64}

The exact state `[q1, q2, p1, p2]` at time `t` of the orbit that starts at
`kepler_initial(e)` at `t = 0` (GM = 1, semi-major axis 1, period 2*pi).

Solve Kepler's equation `E - e*sin(E) = M` for the eccentric anomaly `E`,
where the mean anomaly is `M = t` reduced to [-pi, pi] (use
`rem2pi(t, RoundNearest)`), by Newton's method from `E = M + 0.85*e*sign(sin(M))`
until the update is below `4*eps()` (at most 50 iterations). Then

    q = (cos(E) - e,  sqrt(1 - e^2) * sin(E))
    p = (-sin(E),     sqrt(1 - e^2) * cos(E)) / (1 - e*cos(E))
holes.summary: kepler_exact(e, t): the exact Kepler orbit from Kepler's equation

holes.spec:
verlet_step!(q, p, a, h, accel!) -> nothing

One Stormer-Verlet (velocity Verlet, "kick-drift-kick") step of size `h` for
`q'' = accel(q)`, in place:

    p_half = p + (h/2) * a
    q_new  = q + h * p_half
    a_new  = accel(q_new)          # accel!(a, q): the one force evaluation
    p_new  = p_half + (h/2) * a_new

On entry `a` must hold `accel(q)`; on return it holds `accel(q_new)`, ready
for the next step. The method is second order, symmetric (time-reversible)
and symplectic. Allocates nothing.
holes.summary: verlet_step!(q, p, a, h, accel!): one kick-drift-kick Stormer-Verlet step

holes.spec:
propose_step(h, en; safety = 0.9, facmin = 0.2, facmax = 5.0) -> (accept::Bool, hnew::Float64)

The step-size controller. `en` is the step's `error_norm`. The step is
accepted when `en <= 1`. Whatever the verdict, the next step size is

    hnew = h * clamp(safety * en^(-1/5), facmin, facmax)

(`facmax` when `en == 0`). The exponent is 1/5 because the error estimate
`y5 - y4` is the local error of the 4th-order solution, which is O(h^5): the
step that would have given `en = 1` is `h * en^(-1/5)`, and `safety` aims a
little below it. The clamp stops one odd estimate from changing `h` wildly.
holes.summary: propose_step(h, en; ...): accept or reject, and the next step size

holes.spec:
solve_adaptive(f!, y0, (t0, tf); rtol = 1e-6, atol = 1e-6, h0 = nothing,
                   maxsteps = 1_000_000, observe = nothing) -> NamedTuple

Adaptive Dormand-Prince 5(4) from `t0` to `tf > t0`. Returns
`(y, t, nf, naccept, nreject)`: the state at `tf`, the final time (exactly
`tf`), the number of `f!` calls, and the accepted and rejected step counts.

* Evaluate `f(t0, y0)` into a `DP54Cache`'s `k1`; the first step is `h0`, or
  `initial_step(...)` when `h0 === nothing` (one more `f!` call).
* Repeat until `t == tf`: shorten the step to `tf - t` if it would pass `tf`
  (and then set `t = tf` exactly on acceptance, not `t + h`); take a
  `dp54_step!`; judge it with `error_norm(c.err, y, c.ynew, atol, rtol)` and
  `propose_step`. On acceptance move to `c.ynew`, copy `k7` into `k1`
  (first same as last) and call `observe(t, y)` if given; on rejection keep
  `t`, `y` and `k1`. Either way continue with the proposed step, except that
  the step after a rejection may not grow (`facmax = 1`, as DOPRI5 does).
* Throw an `ErrorException` if more than `maxsteps` steps (accepted plus
  rejected) are attempted.

`observe(t0, y0)` is also called once before the first step.
holes.summary: solve_adaptive(f!, y0, tspan; ...): the accept/reject loop that lands on tf
initial_step(f!, t0, y0, f0, atol, rtol): Hairer's starting step size

holes.spec:
fit_order(hs, errs) -> Float64

The observed order of convergence: the least-squares slope of `log(errs)`
against `log(hs)` over all the points given (at least two, all positive).
For errors that behave like `C * h^p` the slope is `p`. Which points to pass
(the fit range) is the caller's decision: points where rounding dominates,
or where `h` is too large for the asymptotic regime, bend the line.
holes.summary: fit_order(hs, errs): least-squares slope of log(error) on log(h)

`1:length(x)` assumes indices start at 1 and are linear. Arrays with other axes exist, and the range is also easy to pair with the wrong array.
Iterate the array's own indices: `for i in eachindex(x)` (or `axes(x, 1)`, or `pairs(x)` when you need both index and value).

rules.fp_risk: Only comparisons with a float *literal* are seen; `a == b` between two float variables needs types and is not flagged. `x == 0.0` is sometimes exactly what is meant (guarding a division), so outside `@test` this is ADVICE; inside `@test` it is WARN because tests must state a tolerance (invariant 9).
hints: Is the value on the other side of this comparison computed with rounding? If so, how close to the literal is it guaranteed to be?
Most decimal literals (0.1, 0.3) are not exactly representable in binary, and computed floats carry rounding error, so exact equality can fail for a correct computation (try `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3`).
Compare with a tolerance you can justify: `isapprox(a, b; rtol = ...)` or `a ≈ b`, and write down where the tolerance comes from.

A non-`const` global can be rebound to a value of any type at any time, so code that reads it cannot be specialised on its type: every use is a dynamic lookup, and the function's return type often becomes `Any`.
Declare it `const` if it never changes, or pass it in as an argument (then the function is specialised on its type).
